headline: Setting-up VCPs beat the equal-weight market by +4.6% over 3 months on average, against +1.4% for the classic scanner and +0.6% for plain breakouts
intro: Every base the scanner would have listed, recreated day by day on NSE daily prices from 2005 to October 2026 (liquid stocks: price ₹20+ and median turnover ₹1 crore+ a day), and what the stock did next. A stock setting up gets a buy-stop at its pivot for 20 sessions (cancelled if it falls under the contraction low first); a breakout is bought at the next open. “3-month edge” = the stock's 63-session return after 0.25% costs minus the average liquid stock's over the same days.

findings: Relative strength does most of the work. With no RS check the same bases beat the market by +1.5%; RS 70+ +3.4%, RS 80+ +4.6%, RS 90+ +6.0% (fewer bases). Minervini asks for RS 70+, ideally 80–90+.

How strictly contractions are counted is what matters. Counting every 5% swing (high to low) and asking each to be shallower than the last gave +4.6%; counting only 7% swings +2.1%, and only swings confirmed by a close +1.8% — looser counting lets in bases that are not really tightening. The strict version finds mostly short bases (median 14 sessions, 2–4 weeks): tight, orderly pullbacks after a strong run. Long, loose bases rarely pass.
Lows that do not undercut matter. Letting a later contraction break the previous low cut the edge from +4.6% to +3.0%.
Volume dry-up helps a little. Without it: +4.2%; with the last 5 sessions at 0.8× the 50-day average or less: +4.6%.
A big prior advance is the strongest extra filter. Stocks that had risen 100%+ into the base: +6.7% (476 bases) — an option on the page, not the default, because it leaves few names.
Breakout volume: 1.4×+ (O'Neil's 40–50% rule) +4.4% (227 breakouts); any volume +3.8%; 2.5× (the classic scanner's rule) +3.7% but only 79 breakouts.

The stop decides whether the edge is usable. A stop at the last contraction's low is only a few percent away (median 3.6%) and was hit by ordinary noise: with a 2R target the trades made +0.11% each. An 8% stop with no target, held 63 sessions, made +4.46% a trade (36% winners); a +20% target halved that (+2.35%).
The market matters. With the average liquid stock above its 200-day average: +5.5% a trade (1105); below it: +0.5% (300).

Lumpy, not steady. Most of the gain came in strong years (2014, 2021, 2023); several years lost money (2024 and 2025 among them). Use it with the market check and position sizing, not as a stand-alone signal.

Shrinking contractions add little once the other checks are on (+4.4% without the rule, +4.6% with it), but they are what makes a VCP; with RS 70+ alone, dropping the rule cut the edge from +1.9% to +0.9%.
method: Bases are found with a 5% zigzag; the test used exactly the rules of the scanner (same code, ported line by line and checked on 3,000 random stock-days). DEV = 2005–2015, HOLD = 2016–2026: the rules were chosen from published VCP descriptions before testing, the thresholds were checked on both halves.
limits: Only stocks listed today are in the price history (delisted companies are missing, which flatters every result a little). Fills at the pivot assume the order fills at the pivot or the open if it gaps over. Fewer than 100 bases a year before 2016. Past results, not a promise.
sources: Mark Minervini, Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard (2013) and Think & Trade Like a Champion (2017) — summarised by ChartMill
